domain: Structures, thermal, power and large space infrastructure

bottlenecks.name: Qualification evidence, margins and model credibility
bottlenecks.description: Proving primary structure will not fail. Practice stacks deterministic factors of safety (ultimate ~1.25 uncrewed, ~1.4 crewed, general), empirical buckling knockdown factors from 1960s lower-bound curves (NASA SP-8007; a universal 0.65 for composites that NASA itself calls possibly unconservative), building-block test pyramids from coupons to full-scale static tests, and model-credibility processes (NASA-STD-7009). Each dedicated qualification article costs months to years.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~25% of structures/thermal engineering effort on a new vehicle or large spacecraft (analyst estimate, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: High for the math, capped for the payoff. Worst-case imperfection theory and model-form error are genuinely open; reliability-based margins, rare-event estimation and certified error bounds are solved in principle but expert-scarce, which is exactly what on-demand AI supplies. Standards bodies and agencies gate the benefit, so downstream nodes are capped at Medium.

bottlenecks.name: Launch loads and dynamics
bottlenecks.description: Coupled loads analysis (CLA) cycles with the launch provider using Craig-Bampton component models, repeated as designs mature; random vibration, acoustic and shock environments enveloped from flight data plus fixed margins; the mid-frequency band where neither finite elements nor statistical energy analysis is reliable. NASA NESC built Norton-Thevenin Receptance Coupling (2023-2024) precisely because full CLA is slow and costly.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium-High. CLA setup and model reduction are expert-scarce routine work that AI agents can run on demand (fast, P1); the mid-frequency problem is open applied math (slower, P6). Forcing-function uncertainty (liftoff acoustics, buffet) and mandatory qualification-by-test remain.

bottlenecks.name: Damage tolerance, fatigue and inspection for reuse
bottlenecks.description: Crack growth and composite damage under the low-cycle, high-amplitude, cryogenic and thermal-cycling spectra of reusable stages; COPV liner cracks; non-destructive inspection turnaround between flights; qualifying structural health monitoring (SHM) with a probability of detection. First stages are ~70% of launch-vehicle cost (ONERA, 2026), so reuse economics hinge on inspection cost.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~15% and rising with reuse (analyst estimate, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium. Inverse-problem stability, optimal sensor placement and model-assisted POD are solved in principle but expert-scarce (AI helps quickly). Damage physics is data-limited: theory needs coupon-to-subcomponent test campaigns. Catalog families 372, 365, 366 touch this only through confidence (P5) and one ceiling (P3).

bottlenecks.name: Thermal design and heat rejection
bottlenecks.description: Radiator sizing under the Stefan-Boltzmann T^4 law with view factors to Earth, Sun and the spacecraft itself; heat transport (pumped liquid and two-phase loops, heat pipes) whose microgravity behavior is still correlation-based; thermal-model correlation after thermal-vacuum tests; the chip-temperature versus chip-life trade. For compute satellites thermal is now a primary mass term: ~25% of SpaceX AI1's reconstructed 2.1 t (33FG, Jun 2026).
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~20%, much higher on orbital compute programs (analyst estimate, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium. Radiator and loop design optimization and model correlation are expert-scarce and well-posed (AI helps fast). The physics is fixed (T^4, junction-temperature limits) and the binding gates are manufacturing at Starlink volume and flight data for two-phase models. Family 369 (hot spots) is a nil link.

bottlenecks.name: Large deployables and in-space assembly
bottlenecks.description: Deployment reliability of booms, membranes and panels; the impossibility of representative 1 g ground tests for 100 m to km structures; nonsmooth contact and friction dynamics, membrane wrinkling, thermally induced vibration; robotic assembly. ACS3 (2024) flew an ~80 m2 sail on 7 m booms; follow-on booms target 2,000 m2.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium-Low. Better models and scaling laws help, but qualification needs flight data, and formation flying (Google Suncatcher's 81-satellite 1 km cluster; SpaceX Starmind's ~10-satellite clusters) is displacing monolithic km-scale structures.

bottlenecks.name: Power-system integration (fission and very large solar)
bottlenecks.description: For Fission Surface Power: reactor, shield, closed Brayton converter, 500-600 K radiators and lander integration within ~6 t (reactor) on a heavy lander, with radiation transport for shielding (outside the release) and nuclear launch approval. For orbital compute: solar array areal density, which 33FG identifies as AI1's primary mass constraint (ROSA-class 1.8-2 kg/m2 needed).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Low-Medium. Multiphysics trades accelerate, but fuel, licensing, nuclear ground testing, heavy-lander availability and solar-cell/array manufacturing dominate. First-of-a-kind designs freeze before AI design capability matures.

nodes.title: AI-ready structural and thermal test data
nodes.description: Machine-readable databases of the physical evidence this domain runs on: shell-buckling tests with measured imperfections, fatigue and crack-growth spectra, thermal-vacuum correlation sets, microgravity two-phase flow data and deployment telemetry, opened to AI models inside agencies and large firms.
nodes.status_oct2026: Fragmented. NASA Shell Buckling Knockdown Factor (SBKF) test reports sit in NTRS as PDFs; Wagner and Huehne released Monte Carlo knockdown databases and code on Zenodo (Jul 2026); ISS flow boiling and condensation datasets were published 2024-2025; most company data are proprietary or export-controlled (general).
nodes.why: Analyst position (g): this domain is limited by modeling fidelity, data and verification cost, not conjectures. Every physics node below (damage, two-phase flow, deployment, mid-frequency vibration) is data-gated: an AI that can build theory still needs validated tests with known uncertainties. Organizing existing evidence is cheap compared with new tests (a single 8-ft shell test or thermal-vacuum campaign takes months); under S2 the incentive to make data AI-readable is strong, so large organizations do it internally by 2028.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Export control, proprietary interest and poor metadata in legacy tests (unmeasured imperfections, uncertain boundary conditions) mean much historical data cannot validate anything; new tests are still needed.
nodes.signpost: NASA or ESA releases a structured, AI-queryable buckling, fatigue or thermal test database, or a major launch company says it validates models on its full flight-test archive, by 2028.

nodes.title: Firmer math under elasticity, crack and inspection models
nodes.description: Independent confirmation of the release's elasticity and fracture results: smooth isotropic Lame moduli are uniquely determined by boundary measurements (372); metric and connection recovery from one boundary patch, with conductivity nonuniqueness (365); regularity of planar Mumford-Shah crack sets (366); the 3D Ball-Evans approximation problem (368).
nodes.status_oct2026: 372, 366 and 368 are T1 (manuscript only). 365 is T3 (agent-written Lean proof in the repo, unchecked by outsiders). No outside Comparator report as of 2026-10-07. PDE formalization is weak in the release (3 of 16 PDE families).
nodes.why: These four families are the release's only direct contact with structural mechanics. 372 tells inspection engineers that full boundary data determine elastic stiffness in principle; it says nothing about how stably, and Calderon-type problems are typically only logarithmically stable (general), so it raises confidence without changing tools. 366 underpins the Griffith/Francfort-Marigo variational fracture energies behind phase-field fracture codes: minimizing crack sets are well-behaved in 2D. 368 is a technical tool for nonlinear-elasticity existence and approximation theory (invertible deformations), relevant to large-deformation finite elements. The conductivity-nonuniqueness half of 365 is a negative result: some conductivities cannot be recovered from one boundary patch, a potential ceiling for electrical-resistance damage sensing in carbon-fiber structures (conditional on the T3 premise and on the counterexample class being physically relevant). Under S2, AI-assisted formalization of PDE catches up (2028), so confirmation by 2031 is likely.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Engineers already run elastography, guided-wave inversion and phase-field fracture codes without these theorems; uniqueness in principle is not stability; the counterexamples may live in coefficient classes (rough, anisotropic, non-generic) that real laminates never present.
nodes.signpost: An independent Comparator run on 365, or inverse-problems specialists endorsing 372 in a refereed venue, by end-2027; any SHM paper using 365's nonuniqueness construction to bound resistance-based damage sensing.

nodes.title: Hot spots conjecture (planar case) confirmed
nodes.description: Family 369 claims that on any simply connected planar domain, the slowest-decaying non-constant temperature mode of an insulated (Neumann) plate takes its maximum and minimum on the boundary, settling Rauch's 1974 conjecture for that class.
nodes.status_oct2026: T1 (manuscript only). Human literature in 2025-2026 proves only special classes (lip-type and symmetric domains in higher dimensions, TAMS-B Apr 2026; convex hyperbolic domains with small eigenvalues; trapezoids and kites). A certified-numerics project (cert-machine, Zenodo, Oct 5 2026, not refereed) certified a non-symmetric convex trapezoid case.
nodes.why: A dead-end leaf for engineering, included to show the mapping honestly. Real radiators and panels are 3D, multi-material, with radiative (not insulated) boundaries, and thermal engineers compute their modes numerically for every geometry. The theorem confirms an intuition (slowest insulated thermal mode peaks at edges) and could inform sensor-placement heuristics for thin insulated plates; it changes no design. Effect on space thermal engineering: nil to negligible.
nodes.strongest_case_small: This node is itself the strongest case: radiative boundary conditions, 3D geometry and numerical design make the planar Neumann theorem irrelevant to hardware.
nodes.signpost: Expert acceptance (refereed version or endorsement by spectral-geometry specialists) by 2027. No engineering signpost is expected.

nodes.title: Worst-case imperfection theory for thin shells
nodes.description: Rigorous answers to the open question of which manufacturing imperfections (shape, amplitude, number, location) most reduce the buckling load of thin cylinders and cones, with provable lower bounds on the knockdown factor given a factory's measured imperfection statistics.
nodes.status_oct2026: Genuinely open. Ubamanyu, Blond, Hutchinson and Reis (arXiv, Jul 2026) show the localized dimple, nearly worst-case for spheres, is not worst-case for cylinders, and find a statistical size effect; Wagner et al. (Proc. R. Soc. A, 2025) propose a regime-aware mechanistic design curve; the 1960s SP-8007 lower bounds remain the reference.
nodes.why: This is a nonconvex variational and stochastic problem in nonlinear shell theory (Koiter asymptotics, energy barriers, extreme-value statistics of defect populations): bespoke research-grade applied math of the kind S2 makes routine by 2028. A provable lower bound tied to measured imperfection spectra is what lets designers replace empirical lower-bound curves with tighter, defensible knockdowns (see struct-shell-knockdown-rules).
nodes.strongest_case_small: Humans are converging anyway (mechanistic design curve, probabilistic knockdowns, SBKF); boundary conditions and load imperfections, not geometric theory, drive much of the test scatter; any bound is only as good as one factory's imperfection data.
nodes.signpost: A paper (AI-assisted or not) proving worst-case imperfection families, or computing certified lower bounds, for axially compressed cylinders by 2028.

nodes.title: Structural margins with certified uncertainty bounds
nodes.description: Reliability-based structural margins with rigorous rare-event probability estimates and quantified model-form error, as a defensible alternative to stacked deterministic factors (ultimate factors of ~1.25-1.4, model-uncertainty factors, test factors).
nodes.status_oct2026: Practice is deterministic factors of safety (NASA-STD-5001 family, general) plus model-credibility assessment (NASA-STD-7009); probabilistic design used selectively. The release contains nothing on uncertainty quantification. 139 (subpolynomial-query log-concave sampling, Lean, T3) is theory for the posterior sampling such methods use.
nodes.premise_tier: n/a (139 is T3 but peripheral; constants unknown, so P4 effect marginal)
nodes.why: Reliability methods, multifidelity Monte Carlo and Bayesian calibration are largely solved in principle but expensive and expert-scarce per program; model-form error and high-dimensional rare events remain open. On-demand AI applied math makes doing this properly on every program affordable. Replacing a stacked factor of ~1.4 with a reliability-equivalent margin is typically worth several percent to ~10% of primary-structure mass (general).
nodes.strongest_case_small: Factors of safety cover unknown unknowns (workmanship, unmodeled load paths) that no UQ captures; crewed-system safety organizations will keep deterministic factors; the method is not the bottleneck, test data are.
nodes.signpost: NASA or ESA publishes a probabilistic structural design standard or handbook revision allowing reduced factors with quantified reliability, or a launch provider reports using certified UQ margins, by 2029.

nodes.title: Closing the mid-frequency vibration gap
nodes.description: Error-controlled prediction of launch vibroacoustic response in the mid-frequency band (roughly a few hundred Hz to ~1-2 kHz), where finite-element models are too costly and statistical energy analysis is invalid, via hybrid FE-SEA and reduced-order models with a posteriori error bounds.
nodes.status_oct2026: A long-standing open problem (general); practice envelopes predictions with margins and relies on acoustic and random-vibration tests. NASA NESC's Norton-Thevenin Receptance Coupling (2023-2024) cuts the cost of coupled loads analysis but does not address mid-frequency fidelity.
nodes.why: Mid-frequency is hard because modal and statistical descriptions both break down. AI can design and prove error estimators for hybrid methods quickly under S2, but validation needs reverberant-chamber and flight data with quantified uncertainty. If solved, component random-vibration levels could be set from prediction with smaller margins, feeding struct-launch-env-margins.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Qualification by test remains mandatory; uncertainty in the forcing (liftoff acoustics, transonic buffet) dominates structural model error, so even perfect structural models leave most of the margin in place.
nodes.signpost: A hybrid FE-SEA method with proven error bounds, validated against chamber data, ships in a commercial vibroacoustics code by 2029.

nodes.title: Damage detection with proven detection limits
nodes.description: Problem-specific stability estimates, optimal sensor placement and model-assisted probability of detection (MAPoD) for guided-wave, strain and electrical-resistance damage sensing, telling engineers what damage size a given sensor layout can and cannot see.
nodes.status_oct2026: MAPoD for guided-wave SHM on composite cryogenic tanks for reusable launchers is active research (ONERA, Jul 2026); SHM is not yet qualified as an inspection replacement on launch vehicles (general). The release supplies uniqueness (372, T1) and nonuniqueness (365, T3) theory and crack regularity (366, T1), not stability constants.
nodes.premise_tier: T3 for the ceiling (365); T1 for 372 and 366 (those contributions conditional)
nodes.why: The question that earns inspection credit is not whether damage is identifiable in principle (372: yes, for smooth isotropic moduli with full boundary data) but how small a delamination N sensors detect at 90/95 confidence. That is quantitative stability plus statistics: solved in principle, expert-scarce, ideal for on-demand AI. Negative results act fastest (P3): 365's conductivity nonuniqueness and typical logarithmic stability mark where resistance-based sensing skins cannot localize damage, steering programs to guided waves or denser arrays. The node's main pathway is capability; the catalog adds confidence and one ceiling.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Real SHM is limited by sensor aging, bonding and temperature/cryogenic compensation, not inverse-problem theory; regulators and operators accept POD from physical specimen tests, not proofs.
nodes.signpost: A launch operator or NASA program reports SHM-based POD curves accepted in place of a scheduled NDE inspection; SHM papers citing 365 or 372 by 2028.

nodes.title: Finite-element solvers with machine-checked error bounds
nodes.description: Structural and thermal finite-element solvers (linear statics, modal, steady conduction-radiation) whose discretization and floating-point errors carry proved bounds (guaranteed a posteriori estimators plus verified arithmetic), so an analysis result ships with a certificate.
nodes.status_oct2026: Guaranteed error estimators exist for model problems (general); verified floating-point toolchains are emerging at flight-software scale (verification domain); nothing at production FE scale; Mathlib coverage of PDE and numerics is thin.
nodes.why: Certification by analysis rests today on solver verification by benchmark plus test correlation. Proof-carrying error bounds remove the code- and solution-verification layer of NASA-STD-7009-style credibility, freeing scarce reviewers for model-form questions. Analyst position (b): formal verification is the bridge to safety-critical use, here applied to numerics rather than flight code.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Discretization error is rarely the dominant uncertainty in structures (joints, boundary conditions, damping and loads are); a certificate on the wrong model is worthless (the specification problem).
nodes.signpost: An open or commercial FE code ships certified error bounds for linear statics or modal analysis with a formal proof artifact by 2029.

nodes.title: Predictive damage and fatigue models for reusable structures
nodes.description: Validated physics-based models of crack growth and composite damage progression under the low-cycle, high-amplitude, cryogenic and thermal-cycling spectra of reusable stages and tanks, replacing conservative empirical scatter factors and knockdowns.
nodes.status_oct2026: No consensus predictive theory for composite failure (general); NASA NESC documented limits of linear elastic fracture mechanics for small cracks in COPV liners (2020); reusable vehicles rely on inspection, fleet-leader experience and conservative life factors (general).
nodes.why: Damage physics is multiscale and data-hungry. AI theory-building (S2, 2029) can propose closures quickly, but each must survive coupon-to-subcomponent test campaigns (months per load spectrum; cryogenic fatigue rigs are scarce). Autonomous labs (S3) compress coupon testing by about a year, not subcomponent and full-scale tests.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Operators already reach reuse by test-fix-fly and inspection, so better theory changes margins not feasibility; composite damage modeling has absorbed decades of expert effort without converging because material variability, not cognition, is the limit. Overlaps the materials domain.
nodes.signpost: A damage model predicts a blind fatigue or residual-strength test series within stated bounds (a successor to the blind-prediction exercise format) by 2029.

nodes.title: Predictive two-phase cooling physics in microgravity
nodes.description: Validated mechanistic models of flow boiling, condensation, critical heat flux and flow-regime transitions in microgravity pumped loops and heat pipes, at the heat fluxes 100-250 kW compute satellites need.
nodes.status_oct2026: Correlation-based. ISS flow boiling and condensation results published 2024-2025 (Int. J. Heat Mass Transfer); microgravity onset-of-boiling studies 2026. Two-phase pumped loops and oscillating heat pipes have flown, but not at AI1's heat flux, quantity or cost (33FG, Jun 2026).
nodes.why: Two-phase transport cuts heat-transport mass (33FG model: ~2.0 kg/kW for Starlink-like transport to ~0.8 kg/kW loop-based) and lets radiators run nearer chip temperature, which matters through T^4. Designers carry margins for microgravity uncertainty. Flight data bind: an ISS campaign yields hundreds of test points, while compute-satellite fleets will stream telemetry from ~2027-28, which S2 AI can turn into models; whoever owns the fleet owns the model.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Engineers design around uncertainty with margin and favorable-orientation ground tests; the margin penalty may be only ~10-20% of heat-transport mass; SpaceX will iterate hardware faster than theory matures.
nodes.signpost: Operator telemetry from AI1 or Starcloud-class two-phase loops published or used in an open model; a microgravity critical-heat-flux model validated within about 15% by 2029.

nodes.title: Predictive simulation of large deployable structures
nodes.description: Validated models of deployment for 50 m to km structures: frictional contact and latching, stored-strain composite booms, tape-spring snap-through, membrane wrinkling and thermally induced vibration, where today's simulations lean on ground tests that gravity corrupts at scale.
nodes.status_oct2026: ACS3 (launched Apr 2024) deployed an ~80 m2 sail on 7 m composite booms; NASA says current booms support sails up to 500 m2 and follow-on booms up to 2,000 m2. Hinge misalignment in over-constrained deployable panels for space solar power is still being quantified (JSME, 2026). Rigid-body Coulomb friction has known existence and uniqueness pathologies (Painleve paradox, general).
nodes.why: At 100 m and beyond, gravity-offload rigs stop being representative, so qualification must be by analysis plus subscale and flight data, which requires models with understood error. AI supplies the math (nonsmooth dynamics, similitude scaling laws, tension-field wrinkling theory) quickly under S2, but validation needs flight deployments, of which there are few per year.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Most deployment failures are workmanship and mechanism problems (snags, stiction, harness routing) that no model predicts; programs mitigate with simplicity and redundancy, not prediction.
nodes.signpost: A 500 m2-plus deployable flies with pre-flight predicted deployment shape and loads matched within stated bounds; NASA flies its follow-on boom technology.

nodes.title: AI agents run and check structural and thermal analysis
nodes.description: AI agents set up, run, check and document finite-element stress, loads, buckling and thermal analyses end to end (meshing, boundary conditions, margins of safety, thermal-model correlation to thermal-vacuum data, coupled-loads cycles), with an engineer signing off.
nodes.status_oct2026: Research prototypes in 2026: LLM agents driving commercial FE codes through MCP (arXiv Sep 2026), multi-agent end-to-end FEA for solid mechanics (arXiv May 2026), PDE-Agents (arXiv Jun 2026). No public flight-program use (general).
nodes.why: Analyst position (a): most engineering math is bespoke and easier than the catalog. The bulk of structures and thermal effort is setup, checking and correlation by scarce senior analysts: solved in principle, expert-scarce. Under S2 an analysis cycle costs several times less; a thermal-model correlation that takes weeks after a test could take days (assumption).
nodes.strongest_case_small: Analysis labor is a minority of program cost; export-control and data-access rules slow adoption at primes; accountability keeps human sign-off time roughly constant.
nodes.signpost: A NASA center, prime or new-space firm says AI agents produce flight-program stress or thermal analysis reports with human sign-off, by 2027-28.

nodes.title: Lighter buckling design rules for tanks and interstages
nodes.description: Analysis-based, mechanistic or probabilistic knockdown factors replace the 1960s lower-bound curves for cylinders and cones (and the universal 0.65 for composites) in agency and industry design practice.
nodes.status_oct2026: NASA SBKF developed and test-validated analysis-based knockdown approaches on 8-ft metallic and composite cylinders (2010s-2022); a NASA review warns the universal 0.65 composite factor can be unconservative; Wagner et al. (2025) report weight savings above 14% and up to 31% in optimized configurations with a mechanistic design curve. Standards adoption is incomplete.
nodes.why: For an unstiffened isotropic cylinder in axial compression the classical buckling load scales with wall thickness squared, so required thickness scales as KDF^-1/2: moving the knockdown from 0.65 to 0.80 cuts buckling-critical wall mass ~10%, to 0.90 ~15%; stiffened, sandwich and optimized shells see 14-31% (Wagner et al.). The math arrives in 2028 under S2; standards revision (SP-8007, ECSS buckling handbook) and validation tests on representative shells bind, so the band is capped at Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Buckling-critical structures (interstages, intertanks, unpressurized barrels, adapters) are a minority of dry mass; new-space firms test to failure and do not follow SP-8007 strictly; a kilogram saved on a booster buys only ~0.1-0.2 kg of payload (general).
nodes.signpost: A NASA SP-8007 or ECSS buckling-handbook revision adopting regime-aware or probabilistic knockdowns, or a launch-vehicle program citing them, by 2029.

nodes.title: Tighter launch vibration and acoustic environments
nodes.description: Component and spacecraft random-vibration, acoustic and shock test levels derived from error-bounded predictions calibrated on flight data, instead of enveloped data plus fixed margins, reducing overdesign and test failures.
nodes.status_oct2026: Environments are enveloped flight data plus fixed qualification margins (for example qualification at acceptance +3 dB, general); NESC's NTRC methods cut coupled-loads cost (2023-2024); each coupled-loads cycle with a launch provider takes weeks (general).
nodes.why: Random vibration sizes brackets, secondary structure and electronics boxes; a 3 dB margin doubles the test PSD (about 1.4x g-rms). With high-cadence vehicles generating flight data and AI building calibrated predictive models, environments can be stated as exceedance probabilities. Launch-provider user guides and agency test standards gate adoption, so Medium is the cap.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Launch providers have little incentive to tighten published environments; forcing uncertainty dominates; savings fall on small parts and test-failure rates rather than vehicle mass.
nodes.signpost: A launch provider publishes environments derived from flight-calibrated predictive models with stated exceedance probability.

nodes.title: AI-optimized radiators and heat transport
nodes.description: Coupled conduction-radiation-two-phase design optimization (panel topology, heat-pipe and loop layout, view factors to Earth and arrays, micrometeoroid segmentation, deployment structure) that reaches ~2.5 kg/m2 panels and ~3 kg/kW thermal-subsystem mass at ~370 K chip temperature.
nodes.status_oct2026: 33FG model: Starlink V3-like thermal ~19.4 kg/kW at 310 K; StarThink V2 ~3.0-3.4 kg/kW at 370 K with 2.5 kg/m2 two-sided panels; proven radiators run 2.5-5 kg/m2, and values below ~5 rest on two-phase hardware not yet flown at this scale. AI1 spec (Jun 2026): 110 m2 deployable liquid radiator at ~1,400 W/m2.
nodes.why: The design space is large but well-posed (T^4 nonlinearity, view-factor coupling, MMOD puncture probability): expert-scarce, ideal for on-demand AI. Assume a 10-25% thermal-mass cut at fixed technology (assumption). At 1,400 W/m2, a GW of waste heat needs ~0.71 km2 of panel, so each 1 kg/m2 of areal density is ~714 t (~7 Starship flights at 100 t) per GW; the AI design gain is ~350-900 t per GW against ~10,000-14,000 t of total satellite mass per GW, i.e. ~2.5-6% of launched mass.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Radiator physics is simple and SpaceX and Starcloud already optimize it with conventional tools; manufacturing cost per m2 at Starlink volume and chip-temperature limits matter more than design insight (33FG: thermal is not a physics blocker).
nodes.signpost: A flown compute satellite discloses radiator areal density below 3 kg/m2; AI1 telemetry shows ~1,400 W/m2 sustained.

nodes.title: Qualification by analysis replaces some structural tests
nodes.description: Agencies and operators accept validated, uncertainty-quantified analysis with certified numerics in place of some static, modal and environmental tests (for example protoflight instead of dedicated qualification units, fewer static test articles for derivative structures).
nodes.status_oct2026: NASA-STD-7009 provides a credibility framework; tests remain mandatory for primary-structure qualification in NASA and ESA practice (general).
nodes.why: A dedicated qualification article for primary structure costs tens of millions of dollars and a year or more (general); each avoided test is a schedule step. Certified UQ plus certified numerics plus AI-run correlation make a credible case for derivatives first. Needs agency acceptance, so capped at Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Test failures routinely expose what analysis missed (joints, workmanship); no agency will drop tests on first-of-kind primary structure; savings concentrate on derivatives.
nodes.signpost: A NASA or ESA program formally grants credit to model-based qualification in place of a planned structural test, by 2029-30.

nodes.title: Second-generation fission power designs
nodes.description: AI multiphysics optimization of reactor, shield, Brayton converter, radiator and lander integration for follow-on fission systems (lower kg/kWe at 100 kWe-plus, Mars or nuclear-electric variants) after the first unit's design is frozen.
nodes.status_oct2026: NASA directive (Jul 31 2025): at least 100 kWe, closed Brayton cycle, heavy lander with up to 15 t available, launch-ready by Q1 FY2030, awards to two providers within six months of the RFP; reactor under ~6 t (New Space Economy, Apr 2026); final RFP expected early 2026. NASA spent over $200M since 2000 on 1-200 kWe concepts without flight readiness (directive).
nodes.why: A timing trap: first-of-a-kind systems with near-term launch dates freeze their designs (PDR ~2027) before AI multiphysics design capability matures (S2 ~2029), so AI-math gains land in second units. Shield design rests on radiation transport, which the release does not touch; AI applied math helps there only under S2.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Space nuclear power is bounded by fuel supply, launch approval, nuclear ground testing and budgets, not design insight; a second-generation program may not be funded before the first unit operates.
nodes.signpost: NASA awards FSP contracts and announces a follow-on (Mars-class or 200 kWe-plus) design study, ideally naming AI-assisted multidisciplinary optimization.

nodes.title: First flight structure sized with AI-certified margins
nodes.description: A launch-vehicle barrel, interstage or large spacecraft primary structure flies after being sized with analysis-based knockdowns and certified uncertainty margins instead of legacy lower bounds, at 10-30% lower mass for its buckling-critical parts.
nodes.status_oct2026: No such flight attributed to AI-derived design rules. Agency programs still reference SP-8007-type knockdowns; new-space firms rely on test-to-failure (general).
nodes.why: Chain: worst-case imperfection theory (2028) -> design rules (2029) -> build and validation test of a flight article (~1 year) -> flight 2030 in S2. S3 gives no gain because the build-and-test cycle binds. Vehicle-level payoff is modest: ~1-3% payload on an upper-stage-limited vehicle (analyst estimate).
nodes.strongest_case_small: Attribution is nearly impossible because companies already push margins via test; vehicle-level mass savings of 1-3% are within normal design-iteration noise.
nodes.signpost: A launch or spacecraft program publicly states that a flown structure was sized with probabilistic or mechanistic knockdowns (by 2030).

nodes.title: Sensor-based inspection credit for reusable stages
nodes.description: Built-in structural health monitoring with quantified probability of detection replaces scheduled teardown or scanning inspection for defined zones of reusable stages or tanks between flights.
nodes.status_oct2026: Demonstrated on specimens and subscale composite cryotanks (ONERA, 2026); an SHM payload for in-flight re-certification was prepared for ISS exposure (SPIE, Apr 2026); no launch vehicle uses SHM as formal inspection credit (general).
nodes.why: Inspection is a large part of reuse cost: non-destructive testing of large structures is slow and access-limited (ONERA, 2026). Proven detection limits plus certified margins let operators set inspection intervals from data. Sensor qualification under thermal-cryogenic aging binds, which no amount of cognition compresses.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Commercial operators set their own regimes and may find visual and borescope inspection plus fleet leaders cheap enough; sensor reliability, not math, limits SHM.
nodes.signpost: An operator or NASA program announces SHM-based inspection credit for a reusable stage or tank by 2029.

nodes.title: 100-kW-class deployable radiators fly on compute satellites
nodes.description: First flights of deployable liquid or two-phase radiators rejecting 100-250 kW per spacecraft (SpaceX Starmind AI1: 110 m2 at ~1,400 W/m2; Starcloud-class follow-ons), on the physical clock and largely independent of AI mathematics.
nodes.status_oct2026: AI1 spec published Jun 2026 (150 kW peak, 120 kW average, 110 m2 radiator, 70 kW/t target, 70 m wingspan); Musk (Oct 1 2026): over 250 kW of solar per Starmind spacecraft, rack near 250 kW average; Starcloud-1 ran an H100 in orbit from Nov 2025; Starship reached orbit on Sep 28 2026 deploying 26 Starlink V3. First AI1 launch date not published (assumption: 2027).
nodes.why: Anchor node for the orbital-compute chain: the hardware arrives regardless, sized with conventional tools. 33FG's reconstruction puts AI1's thermal system at ~532 kg (25% of 2.1 t) and notes that below ~5 kg/m2 it relies on two-phase hardware SpaceX does not yet build in-house. AI-math effects enter on the second iteration.
nodes.strongest_case_small: This node is the counterfactual baseline: everything here happens without any AI mathematics.
nodes.signpost: AI1 launch and published thermal telemetry (sustained ~1,400 W/m2; chip temperature near 85-95 C).

nodes.title: Sub-2.5 kg/m2 radiators in serial production
nodes.description: Two-phase or oscillating-heat-pipe deployable radiators at or below 2.5 kg/m2 planform, running at ~370 K chip temperature, built at Starlink-like volume (thousands of m2 per month).
nodes.status_oct2026: Lab and prototype panels reach ~1.9-3.9 kg/m2 (33FG survey of NASA and industry prototypes); commercial deployables ~3.5-4.9 kg/m2 (Redwire Q-Rad per 33FG); none in mass production at this areal density (general).
nodes.why: Going from 4 to 2.5 kg/m2 at ~1,400 W/m2 saves ~1,070 t of radiator per GW (~11 Starship flights at 100 t). AI design (2028 in S2) shortens iteration; the manufacturing ramp and qualification bind, so S2 and S3 tie at 2029. In S3, AI-run factories make reaching it by 2031 High.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The gain rides on manufacturing learning curves and supplier insourcing, where AI mathematics plays a small role; 70 kW/t may already be economic without it.
nodes.signpost: SpaceX insources two-phase radiator production (33FG expects within a few years of first purchase) and discloses areal density for a Starmind version.

nodes.title: Lightweight 600 K radiators qualified for fission power
nodes.description: Titanium-water or cesium-titanium heat-pipe radiator panels near 3 kg/m2 rejecting the ~230-300 kW of waste heat from a 100 kWe Brayton system, qualified for launch vibration, freeze-thaw and ~10 years of lunar micrometeoroid exposure.
nodes.status_oct2026: A Cs-Ti heat-pipe panel design reaches 2.98 kg/m2 and rejects >56 kWth at 600 K with launch stresses under 10% of yield (JBIS, Jul 2025); ACT's SBIR Phase III work on Ti-H2O/graphite-fiber radiators added freeze-thaw tests and a 10-year lunar MMOD analysis (ICES, Jul 2026); titanium wick treatments studied (AIAA SciTech, Jan 2026).
nodes.why: At ~25-30% Brayton efficiency, 100 kWe means rejecting ~230-300 kWt; at an average radiating temperature near 450 K and ~3 kW/m2 net on the lunar surface (general), that is ~100 m2 and ~300 kg of panel at 3 kg/m2. The technology is on track without AI mathematics; qualification testing and program funding set the date.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The radiator is not the long pole of fission surface power; fuel, licensing and the lander are.
nodes.signpost: FSP provider PDR with radiator qualification test results, 2027-2028.

nodes.title: A 1,000 m2-class solar sail flies
nodes.description: A solar sail of at least ~1,000 m2 (NASA's follow-on boom class targets up to 2,000 m2) flies, qualified substantially by validated deployment simulation plus subscale tests.
nodes.status_oct2026: ACS3 flew ~80 m2 (2024); NASA states current composite booms support up to 500 m2 and follow-on booms up to 2,000 m2; no funded 1,000 m2-class flight mission identified (general).
nodes.why: Better deployment models reduce the risk of scaling 10-25x in area, but the binding gate is a funded mission; sails compete for small science budgets. The math moves the risk, not the money.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Sail scale-up is gated by funding and membrane durability, not modeling; meanwhile 70 m-class compute-satellite arrays (AI1's 70 m wingspan) are flying anyway on the commercial track.
nodes.signpost: NASA or another agency funds a 1,000 m2-plus sail mission by 2028.

nodes.title: Model-and-sensor life management of fully reusable heavy stages
nodes.description: Fully reusable heavy launchers (Starship-class and peers) manage structural life with validated damage models and built-in sensors, sustaining fast turnaround without routine teardown inspection and with life limits set by analysis rather than fleet-leader experience alone.
nodes.status_oct2026: Starship reached orbit on Sep 28 2026 with both stages expended at sea (33FG); booster and ship reuse at scale not yet operational; Falcon-class booster reuse relies on inspection and fleet-leader experience (general).
nodes.why: Needs both inspection credit (2029 in S2) and validated damage physics (2030), then flight hours to build confidence. Fleet experience accumulates only with flights, which no cognition compresses; S3's autonomous labs pull the damage models a year earlier.
nodes.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may reach airline-like turnaround empirically, making the AI-math contribution unmeasurable; operators may never publish how they set life limits.
nodes.signpost: A Starship booster or ship flies 10-plus times with publicly described sensor-based inspection between flights.

nodes.title: 100 kW-per-tonne compute satellites in serial production
nodes.description: Compute satellites at ~100 kW/t (versus AI1's ~70 kW/t design point and a Starlink V3-like ~11 kW/t) built at hundreds to thousands per year.
nodes.status_oct2026: AI1 ~70-71 kW/t on peak power (33FG reconstruction, Jun 2026); 33FG's StarThink V2 reference reaches ~102 kW/t with 2.5 kg/m2 radiators and improved solar; 33FG identifies solar areal density (ROSA-class 1.8-2 kg/m2) as the primary constraint.
nodes.why: Requires lighter radiators (2029) plus lighter solar arrays and denser compute; the AI-math contribution is design optimization of the thermal and structural share (~35% of a 100 kW/t satellite's mass is thermal per 33FG V2). Manufacturing ramp binds, so S3 does not beat S2.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Solar areal density and chip power density move kW/t more than thermal design; 70 kW/t may be good enough economically, removing the push to 100.
nodes.signpost: SpaceX discloses a Starmind version at or above 100 kW/t.

nodes.title: A 100 kWe fission reactor operating on the Moon
nodes.description: A fission surface power system delivering at least 100 kWe operates on the lunar surface (one-year demonstration followed by nine operational years in NASA's plan).
nodes.status_oct2026: Directive targets launch readiness by Q1 FY2030 on a heavy lander; NASA-DOE MOU renewed (Jan 2026); December 2025 executive order calls for a lunar surface reactor ready for launch by 2030; three Phase 1 industry teams (Westinghouse, Lockheed Martin with BWXT and Creare, IX). Award status in Oct 2026 not confirmed in this research.
nodes.why: Scenario-invariant on purpose: the binding gates are a heavy cargo lander able to land ~15 t (itself behind schedule), nuclear launch approval, fuel supply and nuclear ground testing. Launch-ready late CY2029 implies landing 2030-31 at best. AI mathematics does not move licensing or lander schedules, and the first unit's design freezes before AI design tools mature.
nodes.strongest_case_small: This node is the clearest nil chain in the domain.
nodes.signpost: Two-provider FSP award, a ground test of the flight-design reactor, and a heavy-lander cargo landing demonstration.

nodes.title: Kilometre-scale monolithic structure in orbit
nodes.description: A single connected structure at least 1 km across (solar-radiator plane for GW compute, space solar power array or large antenna) deployed or assembled in orbit.
nodes.status_oct2026: Starcloud's white paper (Sep 2024) sketches a 5 GW station with a ~4 km x 4 km array assembled modularly; Google Suncatcher (Nov 2025) instead flies 81 satellites within a 1 km radius at 100-200 m spacing; SpaceX said on Oct 6 2026 that Starmind needs ~10-satellite tight-formation clusters at ~10 Tbps; Chinese space-solar-power truss-assembly robotics is active (2026); Caltech's MAPLE beamed power in orbit (2023) with 50 m unit tiles planned.
nodes.why: Formation flying is replacing structure: guidance, navigation and optical links give km-scale clusters without km-scale structures, so the business case for a monolith weakens even as modeling improves. Deployment physics (2030 in S2) and certification by analysis (2030) arrive too late to fly a funded km-scale structure by 2031.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Even with perfect models, nobody is paying for a monolith when formation flying works; the most likely km-scale builder (Chinese space solar power) runs on its own schedule.
nodes.signpost: A funded km-scale assembly demonstration (for example a Chinese space-solar-power milestone), or an orbital-compute operator abandoning formation flying for a monolith.

nodes.title: Structures and thermal design cycles 3-10x faster
nodes.description: Time from a requirement change to signed-off stress, loads and thermal analysis compresses severalfold across the industry, cutting non-recurring engineering and allowing more design iterations per program.
nodes.status_oct2026: Agentic FEA is at research-prototype stage (2026); coupled-loads and thermal correlation cycles still take weeks (general).
nodes.why: The earliest and most certain effect in this domain. If structures and thermal analysis is ~10-20% of spacecraft non-recurring engineering (general) and agents cut its labor 50-80% (assumption), NRE falls ~5-15%; the larger benefit is more iterations per month, which compounds into lighter, better-margined designs.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Program schedules are bound by hardware procurement and physical tests (thermal vacuum, vibration), not analysis; faster analysis can simply wait longer for the test chamber.
nodes.signpost: Primes or new-space firms report analysis cycle-time reductions, or stress-analyst hiring shifts toward review roles, by 2028.

nodes.title: 5-15% lighter structures on new vehicles and spacecraft
nodes.description: Vehicles and spacecraft designed from ~2028 show 5-15% lower structural mass for equivalent loads, from combined knockdown, uncertainty-margin, launch-environment and optimization gains.
nodes.status_oct2026: No measurable trend attributable to AI mathematics (general).
nodes.why: Needs new designs started after the methods exist (2028-29) to finish qualification and fly; most fleets flying in 2031 were designed earlier. Vehicle-level effect is small: structure saved on an upper stage converts ~1:1 to payload, on a booster ~0.1-0.2:1 (general), so a 10% structural cut is a few percent of payload at most.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Launch economics are set by propulsion, reuse and cost, not structural mass (Starship deliberately uses heavier, cheaper stainless steel); measured mass fractions will not separate AI effects from normal improvement.
nodes.signpost: New vehicle or spacecraft reveals citing AI-derived design rules with disclosed dry-mass fractions.

nodes.title: 1 GW of compute operating in orbit
nodes.description: Cumulative at least 1 GW of compute power in orbit (about 4,000 satellites at ~250 kW, or ~10,000-14,000 t at 70-100 kW/t), rejecting ~1 GW of waste heat through ~0.7 km2 of radiator panel.
nodes.status_oct2026: SpaceX filed for up to 1 million orbital data-center satellites (Jan 2026) and is partnering with Nvidia on Starmind AI1 (Aug 2026); Starcloud raised $170M (Mar 2026); Google Suncatcher plans two prototypes with Planet by early 2027; Starship reached orbit Sep 28 2026. Orbital compute in Oct 2026 is at kilowatt scale (general).
nodes.why: 1 GW at 70-100 kW/t is ~100-140 Starship flights at 100 t. The AI-math share is second-order: lighter radiators and better thermal design save ~350-1,000 t per GW (~3-11 flights), a few percent. Scenario differences mostly reflect compute demand and capital (S2/S3 make orbital compute more urgent), not mathematics. Launch cadence, chip supply and capital bind.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Thermal physics (T^4, junction-temperature limits) is unchanged, and the timing is set by Starship cadence and financing; AI mathematics could vanish from the chain without moving this node by more than months.
nodes.signpost: Starmind production rate and dedicated Starship flights per year; SpaceX reporting deployed orbital compute in hundreds of MW by 2029.

scenario_contrast: S1 (plateau): research-grade applied math reaches outside teams around 2030, so the cognitive tiers (1-4) land 2028 to beyond 2031 and only 7 of 16 are Medium or better by 2031. The early wins are AI agents running routine analysis (2028) and expert confirmation of the elasticity and hot-spots manuscripts; tiers 5-7 are mostly Low or Speculative (4 of 13 Medium or better, two of them hardware anchors that happen without AI math). S2 (exponential, base case): the cognitive clock compresses by about 2 years on average (median tier 1-4 year 2029; all 16 Medium or High by 2031). Worst-case imperfection theory, certified uncertainty margins, SHM detection limits and radiator optimization arrive in 2028; the physics nodes (composite damage, microgravity two-phase flow, deployment dynamics) arrive in 2030 because data, not cognition, binds. The physical tiers move only about 1 year on average (median 2030) because standards revisions, build-and-qualify cycles, sensor qualification, manufacturing ramps and launch cadence bind. By 2031 under S2: lighter buckling rules (Medium), a first flight structure sized with AI-certified margins (Medium, 2030), SHM inspection credit (Medium), 100 kW/t compute satellites (Medium, 2030) and 1 GW of orbital compute (Medium, 2031, with AI math a second-order contributor), while a km-scale monolith stays Speculative and the lunar 100 kWe reactor stays Low in every scenario. S3 (recursive): moves half the cognitive nodes another year (mainly physics nodes through autonomous labs, and verified numerics) but only 4 of 13 physical nodes, by one year each (reusable-stage life management, a 1,000 m2 sail, 1 GW orbital compute, the structural-mass step). It cannot compress orbital exposure, fleet flight hours, heavy-lander schedules, nuclear licensing or standards cycles. Net: in this domain the S1-to-S2 gap is large in analysis labor and design rules, small in flown hardware by 2031; most of the S2 payoff lands in second-generation hardware after 2031.
key_insights: The catalog barely reaches this domain; the capability does. Only five families touch it (372, 365, 366, 368 elasticity and fracture; 369 hot spots), all as confidence (P5) except one possible ceiling: 365's conductivity nonuniqueness (T3) may bound resistance-based damage sensing in carbon-fiber structures. The hot-spots result (369) changes no thermal design.

The largest near-term effect is labor, not theorems: AI agents running and checking stress, loads and thermal analyses (prototypes exist in 2026) compress design cycles severalfold by ~2028 under S2. This is 'solved in principle but expert-scarce' work, and it is the only node that is High by 2031 in every scenario.

The clearest 'lighter primary structure' chain runs through an open applied-math problem, not a famous conjecture: worst-case imperfections in thin shells. Raising a knockdown factor from 0.65 to 0.80 cuts buckling-critical wall mass ~10% (t scales as KDF^-1/2); optimized shells save 14-31% (Wagner et al. 2025). Standards revision and validation tests cap it at Medium, and the vehicle-level payoff is ~1-3% payload.

Uniqueness is not stability. For structural health monitoring, AI-produced problem-specific stability estimates and probability-of-detection curves matter far more than 372-style uniqueness theorems, because inspection credit depends on what damage size N sensors can see at 90/95 confidence.

For orbital data centers, heat rejection is an engineering and manufacturing problem, not a math or physics blocker. Thermal mass per GW falls from ~19,400 t (Starlink-like, 310 K, one-sided) to ~3,400-3,500 t (AI1 or StarThink V2, ~370 K, two-sided) through temperature and architecture choices already made; AI-optimized design adds perhaps a further 10-25% of thermal mass (~350-900 t, or 3-9 Starship flights per GW), i.e. a few percent of launched mass.

First-of-a-kind timing trap: Fission Surface Power (launch-ready target Q1 FY2030) and AI1 (spec published Jun 2026) freeze their designs before S2's AI design-optimization capability (~2029) matures, so AI-math gains land in second-generation units after 2030.

Formation flying is displacing km-scale structures: Google Suncatcher (81 satellites within 1 km) and SpaceX Starmind (~10-satellite tight clusters, Oct 2026) solve the aperture and bandwidth problem with GNC and optical links. A km-scale monolith stays Speculative by 2031 even under S2.

Data, not cognition, gates the physics nodes (composite damage, microgravity two-phase flow, deployment dynamics, mid-frequency vibration). Compute-satellite fleets streaming thermal telemetry from ~2027-28 become the most valuable two-phase dataset in history; whoever owns the fleet will own the models.

Certification by analysis is the biggest prize (each avoided qualification article saves tens of millions of dollars and a year) but sits behind the slowest gate. Verified finite-element numerics (P2) help less here than in flight software because discretization error is rarely the dominant structural uncertainty.

S3 versus S2 barely matters at tiers 5-7 in this domain: S3 moves 4 of 13 physical nodes forward by one year (reusable-stage life management, a 1,000 m2 sail, 1 GW orbital compute, the structural-mass step), mostly because autonomous labs speed damage-model testing, while qualification tests, flight data, manufacturing ramps, nuclear licensing and launch cadence hold the rest. S1 to S2 moves the cognitive tiers about 2 years but the physical tiers only about 1.
nil_effects: Stefan-Boltzmann is not negotiable: radiator area per watt at a given temperature is fixed, and chip junction limits (~85-105 C) cap radiator temperature unless heat pumps spend power to lift it. No theorem changes the ~0.7 km2 of panel per GW at ~1,400 W/m2.
Launch cadence, heavy-lander availability, capital and chip supply set the dates for GW-scale orbital compute and lunar fission power under all three scenarios.
Space nuclear power gates (fuel supply, nuclear launch approval, ground testing, budget) are untouched; radiation transport for shield design is outside the release entirely.
Material strength, stiffness and density limits do not move with mathematics; any gains come from using existing materials closer to their limits (materials domain covers new materials).
Qualification testing of first-of-kind primary structure, thermal-vacuum and vibration tests remains mandatory through 2031; analysis can reduce tests on derivatives, not eliminate them.
Galactic speedups (107 matrix multiplication, 130 FFT) give no speedup to finite-element, vibroacoustic or thermal codes.
Well-posedness theorems (372, 366, 368) change no simulation code; they raise confidence that what the codes approximate exists and is unique.
Family 369 (hot spots) has no effect on radiator or panel thermal design: real hardware is 3D with radiative boundaries and is designed numerically.
Micrometeoroid and debris flux is a property of the environment; mathematics changes only the design response (segmentation, armoring), not the threat to km2-scale radiators.

signposts.event: A research-grade math model becomes publicly available and an aerospace firm reports using it (or an agentic FEA tool) on flight-program structural or thermal analysis, 2027.
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms cap-research-math-public and struct-agentic-analysis-workflows on the S2 clock; absence by end-2027 shifts the tree toward S1 by ~1-2 years.

signposts.event: An independent Comparator run on family 365, or a refereed acceptance of 372 by inverse-problems specialists, by end-2027.
signposts.what_it_changes: Raises struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations to T4 and lets the SHM ceiling argument be stated without the 'conditional' label; an error found would remove the P3 ceiling.

signposts.event: SpaceX AI1 launches and publishes thermal telemetry (sustained ~1,400 W/m2, chip temperature, radiator areal density), 2027.
signposts.what_it_changes: Anchors the orbital-compute chain; areal density below ~3 kg/m2 pulls struct-radiator-lightweight-production and the 100 kW/t fleet forward; trouble with two-phase loops raises the value of struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.

signposts.event: NASA awards Fission Surface Power to two providers and publishes a PDR schedule and lander assumption, 2026-2027.
signposts.what_it_changes: Sets the physical clock for struct-fsp-radiator-qual and struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe; slippage moves the lunar node beyond 2031 in all scenarios.

signposts.event: A NASA SP-8007 or ECSS buckling-handbook revision adopts regime-aware or probabilistic knockdown factors, by 2029.
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms struct-shell-knockdown-rules on the S2 date and opens struct-flown-lighter-structure; continued reliance on 1960s curves keeps the chain at S1 timing.

signposts.event: A paper proves worst-case imperfection families or certified lower bounds for axially compressed cylinders, especially if AI-assisted, by 2028.
signposts.what_it_changes: Direct evidence that S2's cognitive clock is reaching bespoke applied mechanics; failure by 2029 suggests applied math is diffusing at S1 speed.

signposts.event: A launch operator or NASA program accepts SHM-based probability-of-detection curves in place of a scheduled inspection, by 2029.
Starship booster or ship reflights at high cadence with disclosed inspection practice, 2027-2029.
signposts.what_it_changes: Shows whether reuse is reached empirically (shrinking the AI-math contribution) or with model-based life management.

signposts.event: SpaceX or another operator discloses a compute satellite at or above 100 kW/t, or Starmind production above ~1,000 satellites per year, by 2029-30.
signposts.what_it_changes: Pulls struct-100kw-per-tonne-fleet and struct-gw-orbital-compute toward High; persistent ~70 kW/t designs signal that solar areal density, not thermal, binds.

signposts.event: An orbital-compute operator moves from formation-flying clusters to a monolithic km-scale structure, or China funds a km-scale space-solar-power assembly demo.
signposts.what_it_changes: Would revive struct-km-monolith; otherwise the GNC substitution holds and large-structure math stays a niche.
